headline: NATO jets shoot down a drone over Lithuania
summary: NATO fighter jets shot down a drone that crossed into Lithuania early Tuesday, the country's president said. Officials think it came from Belarus, a Russian ally, and don't yet know who sent it. Alerts sounded across the capital, Vilnius. Denmark said Monday a Russian warship fired flares at one of its helicopters over the Baltic Sea.

cover_question.q: Why did they shoot down the drone?

cover_answer: It crossed the line. Nobody knows yet who sent it.
table_question: If someone keeps poking you but never hits, when do you push back?

5-7.script: A drone, a flying robot with no pilot, flew into a country called Lithuania last night. Jets from its friends went up and knocked it out of the sky, the way a goalie blocks a ball before it reaches the net. Nobody knows yet who sent it. The grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: A flying robot and a goalie are things they can picture. Where it came from is not their problem.
5-7.why_long: A drone is a flying robot and a jet is a goalie. That is as much as a five-year-old can do with this, and it is enough: something came, something stopped it. Joanne Cantor found that at this age fear comes from how a thing looks and sounds, so who sent it is not their problem. Yours is the calm voice.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: Just after midnight, a drone crossed into Lithuania, likely from Belarus, a friend of Russia. Italian pilots flying for NATO shot it down. NATO is a buddy system: attack one member and the rest treat it as an attack on all. Nobody has said whose drone it was.
8-12.why: The buddy system is the mechanism.
8-12.why_long: The buddy system is worth more here than the drone. Attack one, you have attacked all of them, and that is a rule a ten-year-old can test against every alliance they meet afterwards. The script names it and stops short of blame. Expect “so is this a war?” Nobody has said whose drone it was.

13-17.script: When does 'not quite war' become war? A drone over Lithuania, a Russian warship firing flares at a Danish helicopter, Polish jets scrambling, all within a day. Poland's foreign minister wants NATO to hit back. Where would you draw the line?
13-17.why: The line-drawing is the whole debate.
13-17.why_long: Three incidents in a day and none of them a war. A teenager can reason about a threshold they have never had to set, which is what the script asks: where is the line, and who draws it? Ask them before you answer. Poland’s foreign minister has an answer and it is worth arguing with.

5-7.a: This one was over Lithuania, an ocean away. Jets there watch the sky for exactly this. The grown-ups have it.

8-12.q: Why did they shoot down the drone?
8-12.a: It flew into Lithuania's airspace uninvited. NATO's job is to guard that airspace, so its jets took it down. Nobody knows yet who sent it.

8-12.q: Is this the start of a war?
8-12.a: No. Nobody has claimed the drone, and Russia hasn't commented. NATO jets have shot down stray drones over Estonia and Latvia this year too.

13-17.a: Nobody has proven who sent it. Poland's foreign minister wants more from NATO. A former US ambassador said: draw the line now.
Moves that stay just short of war: a drone here, flares at a helicopter there. Semafor says the aim is to blur the line between peace and conflict.
